laietani.t: The Iberian people of the coast around Barcelona, known later for the wines of Laietania and their coins minted at Barkeno.
laietani.o: The Laietani lived on the coastal plain and hills between the Llobregat and Tordera rivers, around modern Barcelona and the Maresme, from about the 5th century BCE. They formed part of the Iberian culture of the north-east and traded with Emporion and other Greek ports.
laietani.r: Their society was based on fortified hilltop towns such as Burriac and Puig Castellar, with grain storage silos and craft workshops. They minted coins with Iberian legends, including Laiesken and Barkeno. Under Rome their territory became famous for wine production, mentioned by Pliny and exported in amphorae across the western Mediterranean.
laietani.e: The Laietani were subdued during Cato's campaign of 195 BCE and absorbed into Hispania Citerior. Their hill towns were gradually abandoned for Roman foundations on the plain such as Baetulo, Iluro and, under Augustus, Barcino, the origin of Barcelona.

ligures.t: Ancient peoples of the north-western Mediterranean coast and Alps, from the Arno to the Rhône, who resisted Rome in their mountains for nearly two centuries.
ligures.o: The Ligures were among the oldest recorded peoples of north-western Italy and southern Gaul, already named by Greek writers of the 6th century BCE as living around Massalia and the Gulf of Genoa. Their origins are obscure; their language survives only in place names and personal names, and its relationship to Celtic and other Indo-European languages is debated.
ligures.r: They lived as separate tribes, among them the Ingauni, Intimilii, Apuani and Statielli, in hill forts and upland villages, combining herding, small-scale farming and raiding. Classical authors described them as hardy and poor. They served as mercenaries for Carthage, and along the coast they traded with Greek Massalia and the Etruscans, while inland groups mixed with Celtic neighbours.
ligures.e: Rome fought the Ligures from 238 BCE onward, deporting thousands of Apuani to Samnium in 180 BCE. The last Alpine groups were subdued under Augustus, whose Trophy at La Turbie (7–6 BCE) lists conquered tribes. The region became Augustus's Regio IX, Liguria, a name that survives in the modern Italian region.

lusones.t: A Celtiberian people of the upper Tagus and Jalón, among the first to fight Rome in the Celtiberian wars of the early 2nd century BCE.
lusones.o: The Lusones lived on the high plateau around the sources of the Tagus and the Jalón, between modern Guadalajara and Zaragoza. Appian and Strabo count them among the Celtiberians, and they emerged in the later Iron Age.
lusones.r: Little is known of their society beyond their hillfort settlements and herding economy on the cold uplands. They appear in Roman narratives mainly as a source of fighting men in the wars of the 2nd century BCE.
lusones.e: In 181 BCE they took part in the First Celtiberian War, which ended with the treaty of Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus in 179 BCE. They were drawn into the later wars that ended with Numantia in 133 BCE and were then absorbed into Hispania Citerior.

lordship-of-ireland.t: The territory in Ireland held by English kings as lords of Ireland from Henry II's invasion of 1171 until Henry VIII took the title of king in 1542.
lordship-of-ireland.o: Henry II landed at Waterford in 1171 to control Strongbow and other Norman adventurers. Irish kings and bishops submitted to him, and the papacy endorsed his claim. In 1177 he made his son John Lord of Ireland, a title merged with the English crown when John became king.
lordship-of-ireland.r: The lordship was governed from Dublin by a justiciar or lord deputy, with an Irish Parliament from the 13th century, English common law and shires. Norman lords built castles and towns, but from the 14th century Gaelic recovery and the Black Death shrank English rule to the Pale around Dublin, and the Statutes of Kilkenny of 1366 sought to stop settlers adopting Irish ways.
lordship-of-ireland.e: In 1541 the Irish Parliament declared Henry VIII King of Ireland, creating the Kingdom of Ireland in 1542.

latin-league.t: Alliance of the Latin towns around Rome, bound by shared cults and rights, that fought and then partnered Rome until Rome dissolved it in 338 BCE.
latin-league.o: The Latin peoples of the plain south of the Tiber shared a language, the cult of Jupiter Latiaris on the Alban Mount and other common sanctuaries from the early Iron Age. By the 6th century BCE they met in council at the grove of Ferentina and dedicated a federal shrine of Diana at Aricia, whose founding a Latin dictator, Egerius Baebius of Tusculum, is said to have led.
latin-league.r: The League was a loose association of towns such as Tusculum, Aricia, Lanuvium, Tibur and Praeneste, sometimes led by an elected dictator. Members shared rights of trade and intermarriage with each other. After Rome defeated the Latins at Lake Regillus around 496 BCE, the treaty of Spurius Cassius in 493 BCE made Rome and the League equal partners in defence, and they jointly founded colonies against the Aequi and Volsci.
latin-league.e: As Rome came to dominate the alliance, the Latins revolted in the Latin War of 340–338 BCE. Rome won, dissolved the League in 338 BCE and made separate treaties with each town. The shared 'Latin rights' survived as a legal status Rome later granted to colonies and provinces.

lordship-of-galloway.t: A semi-independent Gaelic lordship in south-west Scotland, whose lords acted almost as kings until the line ended in 1234.
lordship-of-galloway.o: Galloway takes its name from the Gall-Gaidheil, the 'foreign Gaels' of mixed Norse and Gaelic descent who settled the region in the 9th and 10th centuries. Around 1110 Fergus of Galloway emerged as its ruler, styled king in some sources, and married an illegitimate daughter of Henry I of England.
lordship-of-galloway.r: The lords of Galloway ruled a land of cattle and sea-power with its own laws, while founding monasteries such as Dundrennan and Soulseat and reviving the bishopric of Whithorn. Fergus's grandson Roland and great-grandson Alan were great Anglo-Scottish nobles; Alan's fleet raided Ireland and the Kingdom of the Isles.
lordship-of-galloway.e: When Alan died in 1234 without a legitimate son, Alexander II divided Galloway between his daughters, crushing a revolt. The lordship became part of the Kingdom of Scotland; Alan's granddaughter's son was John Balliol.

lordship-of-beaujeu.t: The barony of the Beaujolais hills between Lyon and Mâcon, whose lords founded Villefranche-sur-Saône and served the French crown before it passed to the Bourbons.
lordship-of-beaujeu.o: The lords of Beaujeu appear in the 10th century as castellans in the hills west of the Saône, between the counts of Mâcon and Forez and the archbishops of Lyon. Their castle at Beaujeu gave its name to the Beaujolais, and they gradually brought the surrounding parishes under their control.
lordship-of-beaujeu.r: The lords built a compact barony and around 1140 founded Villefranche-sur-Saône, which became its commercial centre and later capital. Vineyards and the Saône trade underpinned its economy. Lords such as Humbert V, constable of France, rose high in royal service, and the family married into the houses of Forez and Savoy.
lordship-of-beaujeu.e: In 1400 the last lord, Edward II, childless and in debt, left the Beaujolais to Louis II, Duke of Bourbon, and it joined the Duchy of Bourbon. After the Bourbon lands were confiscated in 1527, it passed through several holders before ending up in the Orléans family.

lordship-of-molina.t: A semi-independent Castilian lordship on the borders of Aragon, ruled by the Lara family and governed by its own celebrated fuero.
lordship-of-molina.o: Alfonso I of Aragon took Molina around 1129. It was soon granted to the Castilian noble Manrique Pérez de Lara, who held it under Castilian overlordship and in 1154 gave the town and its land a fuero, a charter of rights for settlers.
lordship-of-molina.r: Molina was a frontier lordship of herders and settlers between Castile and Aragon, defended by its great castle. Its lords issued laws, minted coins and raised troops with considerable autonomy. In the 13th century the heiress Mafalda married the infante Alfonso de Molina, brother of Ferdinand III, tying it closer to the Castilian royal family.
lordship-of-molina.e: Blanca Alfonso de Molina died childless in 1293, and the lordship passed to her half-sister María de Molina, queen of Sancho IV, and thus to the Crown of Castile. Spanish kings still bear the title Lord of Molina.

lordship-of-meath.t: The great Anglo-Norman liberty of Meath granted to Hugh de Lacy, centred on the castle of Trim.
lordship-of-meath.o: In 1172 Henry II granted the former Kingdom of Mide to Hugh de Lacy to balance Strongbow's power in Leinster. De Lacy built motte castles across the territory and began the great stone castle at Trim, which became the largest Norman castle in Ireland.
lordship-of-meath.r: Meath was a liberty with its own courts and officials. De Lacy settled English tenants, founded towns and abbeys and married a daughter of Ruaidri Ua Conchobair, the high king. He was killed at Durrow in 1186. His son Walter de Lacy recovered the lordship after a conflict with King John and held it until 1241.
lordship-of-meath.e: After Walter's death in 1241 the lordship was divided between his granddaughters, creating the liberties of Trim and Meath. Meath later formed the heart of the English Pale.

lebedos.t: Small Ionian city between Teos and Colophon, one of the twelve of the Ionian League, later home of the travelling Dionysiac actors.
lebedos.o: Lebedos was settled by Ionian Greeks, traditionally under Andraemon, son of Codrus, on the coast between Teos and Colophon c. 1000 BCE. Though small, it was one of the twelve members of the Ionian League.
lebedos.r: Little is known of its government. It lived from farming and fishing and had hot springs nearby. Lebedos fell to Lydia and then to the Achaemenid Empire, and paid tribute to Athens as a member of the Delian League. It revolted from Athens in 412 BCE.
lebedos.e: Lysimachus moved many of its inhabitants to Ephesus c. 290 BCE. The Ptolemies refounded it as Ptolemais, and the guild of Dionysiac artists later settled there. Lebedos passed into Roman Asia after 133 BCE; Horace described it as nearly deserted.

lugi.t: People of eastern Sutherland recorded by Ptolemy, whose name may honour the Celtic god Lugus.
lugi.o: The Lugi are known only from Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, which places them in the far north of Scotland, usually located on the east coast of Sutherland around the Dornoch Firth and the Brora area, between the Decantae and the Cornavii (Caithness). Their name may derive from the god Lugus or from a word for raven.
lugi.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or customs. Eastern Sutherland has many brochs along its river valleys and coast, such as those of Strath Brora, suggesting communities led by local families who controlled grazing and farmland.
lugi.e: The Lugi vanish from the record after Ptolemy. Their territory later formed part of the lands of the northern Picts and then of the Norse earldom of Orkney before being drawn into the Scottish kingdom.

lordship-of-valencia.t: The Valencian principality of Rodrigo Díaz, El Cid, who conquered the city in 1094 and held it against the Almoravids until his death.
lordship-of-valencia.o: Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, a Castilian noble exiled by Alfonso VI, had built a mercenary career serving the Taifa of Zaragoza and collecting tribute in the east. When the qadi Ibn Jahhaf killed al-Qadir in 1092, Rodrigo besieged Valencia, which surrendered in June 1094.
lordship-of-valencia.r: El Cid ruled as an independent lord, nominally loyal to Alfonso VI. He defeated Almoravid relief armies at Cuarte in 1094 and Bairén in 1097, burnt Ibn Jahhaf alive and turned the great mosque into a cathedral under Bishop Jerome of Périgord. Most of the Muslim population remained, paying taxes to his garrison.
lordship-of-valencia.e: El Cid died in 1099. His widow Jimena held Valencia until 1102, when Alfonso VI judged it indefensible, evacuated the Christians and burnt the city. The Almoravids entered in May 1102. The story inspired the epic Cantar de mio Cid.

lacetani.t: An Iberian people of inland Catalonia who resisted Rome during the Second Punic War and Cato's campaign of 195 BCE.
lacetani.o: The Lacetani lived in the interior of Catalonia, roughly in the modern comarques of Bages, Anoia and Solsonès, from about the 5th century BCE. They were part of the Iberian culture of the north-east and neighbours of the Ilergetes and Ausetani.
lacetani.r: Their society of fortified hilltop villages lived from farming and herding. Ancient writers, mainly Livy, record them only in wartime, and their name is easily confused with the coastal Laietani, so many details are uncertain.
lacetani.e: They fought the Romans under Gnaeus Scipio in 218 BCE and again in the north-eastern revolt of 197 to 195 BCE, when Cato stormed their chief town. Afterwards they were absorbed into Hispania Citerior and their name faded.

lordship-of-brecknock.t: A marcher lordship in the Usk valley created by Bernard de Neufmarche's conquest of the Welsh kingdom of Brycheiniog.
lordship-of-brecknock.o: Bernard de Neufmarche invaded the kingdom of Brycheiniog in the late 11th century and killed Rhys ap Tewdwr of the Kingdom of Deheubarth near Brecon in 1093. He built Brecon Castle and founded Brecon Priory, granting lands to his followers.
lordship-of-brecknock.r: Brecknock was governed as a marcher lordship with its own courts and military obligations, a Norman lowland lordship over a largely Welsh upland population. It passed by marriage to the de Braose family and then to the de Bohuns, earls of Hereford, and later to the Staffords, dukes of Buckingham.
lordship-of-brecknock.e: Edward Stafford, Duke of Buckingham, was executed in 1521 and the lordship came to the crown. The Laws in Wales Act of 1536 made Brecknock a shire, which survives as part of Powys.

lordship-of-gower.t: A marcher lordship on the Gower peninsula and around Swansea, created by Henry de Beaumont, Earl of Warwick, in the early 12th century.
lordship-of-gower.o: Henry de Beaumont, Earl of Warwick, took Gower from its Welsh rulers around 1106 and built a castle at Swansea. English and Flemish settlers occupied the southern part of the peninsula, which developed a lasting English-speaking character.
lordship-of-gower.r: Gower was divided between an Anglicised lowland 'Englishry' and a Welsh upland 'Welshry'. The lords held their own courts and granted Swansea its first charter. The lordship passed to the de Braose family and later to the Mowbrays and the Herberts, and was repeatedly fought over by the lords of Glamorgan and Welsh princes.
lordship-of-gower.e: The Laws in Wales Act of 1536 attached Gower to the new county of Glamorgan. Its distinct dialect and Anglo-Norman churches remain, and in 1956 it became Britain's first Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.

league-of-corinth.t: Alliance of Greek states under Macedonian leadership created by Philip II after Chaeronea, the framework for Alexander the Great's invasion of Persia.
league-of-corinth.o: After defeating Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BCE, Philip II called the Greek states to Corinth in 338-337 BCE. They swore to a common peace, forbidding wars and revolutions among members, and named Philip hegemon of a war of revenge against Persia. Sparta alone refused to join.
league-of-corinth.r: A council (synedrion) of delegates, with votes roughly proportional to each member's military strength, met at Corinth and other festival sites and could judge disputes. Members kept their own governments, but Macedonian garrisons held Corinth, Thebes, Chalcis and Ambracia. Alexander had his leadership confirmed in 336 BCE and punished Thebes' revolt in 335 BCE in the league's name.
league-of-corinth.e: The alliance gave Alexander a Greek mandate for his Asian campaign. On news of his death in 323 BCE, Athens and the Aetolians led the Lamian War; Antipater's victory at Crannon in 322 BCE ended both the war and the league. Antigonus and Demetrius briefly revived it in 302 BCE.

lusitanians.t: The fierce Iron Age people of central Portugal whose leader Viriathus defeated Roman armies for years before his murder in 139 BCE.
lusitanians.o: The Lusitanians lived between the Douro and the Tagus, in central Portugal and the neighbouring parts of Extremadura, emerging as a recognisable people in the second half of the first millennium BCE. They spoke Lusitanian, an Indo-European language known from a handful of inscriptions in Latin letters, such as those of Cabeço das Fráguas.
lusitanians.r: Lusitanian society was organised in clans and hillfort communities, with warrior bands under chosen leaders and a herding and farming economy in the uplands. Raiding into the richer south was a constant feature. They worshipped local gods such as Bandua and Endovelicus, and their warriors fought in light, mobile formations that troubled Roman legions.
lusitanians.e: After raids from 155 BCE, the Roman praetor Galba massacred thousands under a false truce in 150 BCE. Viriathus, a survivor, led resistance until he was assassinated in 139 BCE, after which resistance collapsed. Their land later became the Roman province of Lusitania, a name later revived as a poetic name for Portugal.

lordship-of-biscay.t: A Basque lordship ruled by the Haro family under Navarre and Castile, whose fueros and assembly at Guernica made it a byword for local liberties.
lordship-of-biscay.o: Around 1040 Íñigo López Ezquerra appears in records as the first count or lord of Biscay, a vassal of Navarre. His descendants, the López de Haro, held the lordship for more than three centuries, moving their allegiance between Navarre and Castile.
lordship-of-biscay.r: The lords ruled with the consent of the Juntas Generales, the general assembly that met under the oak of Guernica and guarded Biscay's fueros, or customary laws. The economy depended on iron mining, forges, shipbuilding and fishing. In 1300 Lord Diego López V de Haro founded Bilbao, which grew into its chief port.
lordship-of-biscay.e: In 1379 the lordship passed by inheritance to John I of the Crown of Castile, and from then on the kings of Castile ruled Biscay as lords. Its fueros survived until the 19th century.

leuci.t: Gallic people of southern Lorraine around Toul, steady suppliers of grain to Caesar's armies.
leuci.o: The Leuci lived on the upper Moselle and Meuse, in the modern departments of Meurthe-et-Moselle and Vosges. Caesar mentions them among the peoples who supplied his army with grain in 58 BCE.
leuci.r: Nothing is known of their rulers. Their land included sanctuaries that grew important under Rome, above all Grand, a great healing shrine of Apollo Grannus with a large mosaic and amphitheatre.
leuci.e: The Leuci seem to have stayed loyal during the revolts, and Rome gave them the status of a free civitas. Their chief town Tullum became Toul, later one of the Three Bishoprics.

locri-epizephyrii.t: Greek city in Calabria famed for the law code of Zaleucus, the earliest written Greek laws, and for its sanctuary of Persephone.
locri-epizephyrii.o: Locrians from central Greece founded Locri Epizephyrii, 'Locri of the West Wind', around 680 BCE on the Ionian coast of Calabria, near Cape Zephyrion. Ancient writers said the settlers included slaves and women of noble families, a story that may reflect the status of women in the city's aristocracy.
locri-epizephyrii.r: Locri's laws, attributed to Zaleucus in the mid-7th century BCE, were reckoned the first written code in the Greek world and known for severe punishments. A council of a thousand governed the city. Its Persephone sanctuary yielded hundreds of painted terracotta plaques (pinakes). Locri defeated much larger Croton at the Sagras river and founded Hipponion and Medma. It was Syracuse's closest ally: Dionysius I married a Locrian woman, and Dionysius II ruled the city harshly from 356 to 346 BCE.
locri-epizephyrii.e: Locri became a Roman ally after the Pyrrhic War, went over to Hannibal and was retaken by Scipio in 205 BCE; the outrages of its commander Pleminius caused a scandal in Rome. It continued as a Roman town until abandoned in the early Middle Ages.

lindos.t: The greatest of the three old cities of Rhodes, crowned by the sanctuary of Athena Lindia and ruled by the sage Cleobulus.
lindos.o: Dorian Greeks settled Rhodes in the early Iron Age, forming three cities, Lindos, Ialysos and Kamiros. Lindos, on the east coast with the island's best natural harbours, grew around its acropolis sanctuary of Athena, and joined the Dorian Hexapolis with Knidos, Kos and Halicarnassus.
lindos.r: Lindian sailors founded Gela in Sicily with Cretans in 688 BCE and traded with Egypt and the Levant. In the 6th century BCE Cleobulus, counted among the Seven Sages, ruled as tyrant and rebuilt the temple of Athena. Lindos later fell under the Achaemenid Empire and then belonged to the Delian League.
lindos.e: In 408 BCE Lindos joined Ialysos and Kamiros to found the new city of Rhodes, which became the island's capital. Lindos remained a religious centre: the Lindian Chronicle of 99 BCE lists famous offerings to Athena, and the acropolis is still a landmark.
lindos.re: Greek religion; cult of Athena Lindia

lingones.t: Gallic people of the Langres plateau around the sources of the Seine and Marne, who stayed loyal to Rome during the great revolt of 52 BCE.
lingones.o: The Lingones held the uplands around Andematunnum (Langres), between the Sequani, the Aedui and the Leuci, astride the watershed between the Seine and Saône basins. Livy and Polybius record that part of the people joined the Celtic migrations into Italy around 400 BCE and settled near the Adriatic coast south of the Po.
lingones.r: Like their neighbours they lived in fortified oppida, struck their own coins and profited from the routes linking the Saône with the Seine. Little is known of their institutions, but they were large enough to supply Caesar's armies with grain.
lingones.e: The Lingones refused to join Vercingetorix in 52 BCE and were rewarded with the status of an allied civitas under Rome. In 70 CE their nobleman Julius Sabinus joined the revolt of the Batavi and proclaimed himself Caesar; after its failure his wife Epponina hid him for nine years before both were executed.

lordship-of-montpellier.t: The merchant town of Languedoc whose Guilhem lords founded a dynasty, whose university taught medicine, and where King James I of Aragon was born.
lordship-of-montpellier.o: In 985 the count of Melgueil granted lands at Montpellier to a man named Guilhem, whose descendants, all named William, ruled the growing town as lords. Montpellier rose quickly in the 11th and 12th centuries as a market and staging post on the road from Italy to Spain.
lordship-of-montpellier.r: The lords governed with an active merchant community and a strong consulate. Montpellier traded spices, cloth and dyes across the Mediterranean, and its medical school, recognised as a faculty in 1220, became one of the most famous in Europe. In 1204 the heiress Marie of Montpellier married Peter II of Aragon; their son James I was born there in 1208.
lordship-of-montpellier.e: The lordship passed to the Aragonese crown and then to the Kingdom of Majorca. In 1349 the hard-pressed James III of Majorca sold Montpellier to Philip VI, and it joined the Kingdom of France.

lordship-of-glamorgan.t: The largest of the Welsh marcher lordships, seized from the last Welsh king of Morgannwg by Robert Fitzhamon and ruled from Cardiff Castle.
lordship-of-glamorgan.o: Around 1093 Robert Fitzhamon overthrew Iestyn ap Gwrgant of the Kingdom of Morgannwg and built a castle at Cardiff inside the old Roman fort. He granted manors in the fertile Vale of Glamorgan to his knights, while Welsh lords kept the uplands.
lordship-of-glamorgan.r: Glamorgan was a marcher lordship, held outside the ordinary English shire system with its own courts and military power. Through inheritance it passed to the earls of Gloucester, notably the Clare family, who built the vast Caerphilly Castle in the 1260s against Llywelyn ap Gruffudd. It later passed to the Despensers, Beauchamps and Nevilles.
lordship-of-glamorgan.e: The Laws in Wales Act of 1536 abolished the marcher lordships, and Glamorgan became a shire of the Kingdom of England, with Cardiff its county town.

leontini.t: Inland Chalcidian city of eastern Sicily on a rich grain plain, whose envoy Gorgias drew Athens into Sicilian affairs in 427 BCE.
leontini.o: Thucydides records that Chalcidians from Naxos, led by Theocles, founded Leontini in 729 BCE, expelling the native Sicels from the site. It lay on hills above the Leontine plain, one of the most fertile grain-growing areas in Sicily, a short distance inland from the sea.
leontini.r: Leontini's wealth came from grain. Around 610 BCE Panaetius became the first known tyrant in Sicily there. The city fell under Hippocrates of Gela around 495 BCE and later under Syracuse. Under pressure from Syracuse it sent the orator Gorgias to Athens in 427 BCE, and his speeches won an Athenian alliance and the first Athenian expedition to Sicily; Gorgias also helped bring Sicilian rhetoric to Greece.
leontini.e: In 422 BCE the Leontine aristocrats expelled the common people and moved to Syracuse, which absorbed the city. Its plight was a pretext for the great Athenian expedition of 415 BCE. Leontini was later revived as a dependent town and as Lentini survives today.

lordship-of-leinster.t: The vast Anglo-Norman liberty in south-east Ireland won by Strongbow, whose division in 1247 created the counties of Leinster.
lordship-of-leinster.o: Diarmait Mac Murchada, deposed king of Leinster, sought Norman help and promised his daughter Aoife and succession to Richard de Clare, Strongbow. After Diarmait's death in 1171 Strongbow claimed Leinster, and Henry II granted it to him as a lordship under the crown in the Lordship of Ireland.
lordship-of-leinster.r: Strongbow and his successors settled knights, founded towns and built castles such as Kilkenny and Ferns. William Marshal, who married Strongbow's daughter Isabel, developed New Ross, Kilkenny and many abbeys, and granted Kilkenny its charter. The lordship had its own courts, exchequer and seneschal.
lordship-of-leinster.e: The five sons of William Marshal all died without heirs, and in 1247 the liberty was divided among his daughters' heirs, forming Carlow, Kilkenny, Wexford, Kildare and part of Laois. The Butler earls of Ormond later held much of it.

lobetani.t: An obscure Iberian or Celtiberian people of the Teruel highlands, known almost only from the geographer Ptolemy.
lobetani.o: The Lobetani are recorded mainly by Ptolemy in the 2nd century CE, who places them in the mountains of eastern Spain with a town called Lobeton, perhaps near Albarracín in modern Teruel. Their origin and language are unknown.
lobetani.r: Nothing is known of their society beyond a probable highland economy of herding, and archaeology cannot securely identify their settlements.
lobetani.e: Their territory was absorbed into Hispania Citerior during the Roman conquest of the interior in the 2nd century BCE. They are remembered only as a name in the ancient geographies.

lexovii.t: Gallic people of the Pays d'Auge in Normandy, whose name survives in the town of Lisieux.
lexovii.o: The Lexovii lived between the Seine estuary and the Orne, with a coastline on the Channel. Caesar names them among the peoples of the Atlantic seaboard.
lexovii.r: Caesar records that in 56 BCE they killed their senators, who would not support war, and joined the coalition of Viridovix, showing a council of nobles similar to those of their neighbours.
lexovii.e: Defeated by Quintus Titurius Sabinus in 56 BCE, they also sent troops to Alesia in 52 BCE. Under Rome their chief town was Noviomagus Lexoviorum, the origin of Lisieux, later a bishopric.
